items.heading: Minor cuts and small wounds
details: Rinse the wound gently under clean running water to remove dirt.
Apply light pressure with a clean cloth to stop any bleeding.
Apply a pinch of turmeric powder directly on the wound - it has natural antiseptic properties.
Cover with a clean bandage and keep the area dry.
See a doctor if bleeding does not stop within 10 minutes, the cut is deep, or it shows signs of infection such as redness, swelling, or pus.

items.heading: Minor kitchen burns
details: Hold the burnt area under cool, not ice-cold, running water for 10-15 minutes.
Do not apply ice, butter, or toothpaste - these can worsen the burn.
Cover loosely with a clean, non-stick cloth or bandage once cooled.
Take a mild pain reliever if needed for discomfort.
Seek medical help for burns larger than a palm, on the face, hands, or joints, or if blisters break or look infected.

items.heading: Bruises
details: Apply a cold compress or ice pack wrapped in cloth for 15-20 minutes to reduce swelling.
Elevate the bruised area if possible.
After 48 hours, switch to a warm compress to improve blood flow and speed healing.
See a doctor if the bruise is very large, unusually painful, or from a significant injury.

items.heading: Insect bite or bee sting
details: If a stinger is visible, scrape it out sideways with a card edge rather than squeezing it, which can release more venom.
Wash the area with soap and water.
Apply a cold compress to reduce swelling and itching.
A paste of baking soda and water can help soothe itching.
Seek emergency help immediately if there is difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or dizziness - signs of a severe allergic reaction.

items.heading: Nosebleed
details: Sit upright and lean slightly forward, not backward, to avoid swallowing blood.
Pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for 10 minutes without releasing to check.
Apply a cold compress to the bridge of the nose.
See a doctor if bleeding does not stop after 20 minutes, or if it was caused by an injury.

items.heading: Minor sprain - the RICE method
details: Rest the injured area and avoid putting weight on it.
Ice it with a cloth-wrapped ice pack for 15-20 minutes every few hours for the first 48 hours.
Compress gently with an elastic bandage, not too tight.
Elevate the injured limb above heart level when possible.
See a doctor if there is severe pain, inability to move the joint, or a visible deformity.

items.heading: Sunburn
details: Take a cool, not cold, shower or apply a cool damp cloth to the affected area.
Apply pure aloe vera gel to soothe and hydrate the skin.
Drink extra water to stay hydrated, and avoid further sun exposure.
Do not pop any blisters that form; keep them covered loosely.
See a doctor for widespread blistering, fever, or signs of heat illness.

items.heading: Choking in an adult - the Heimlich maneuver
details: Ask "Are you choking?" - if they cannot speak, cough, or breathe, act immediately.
Stand behind the person, wrap your arms around their waist, and tip them forward slightly.
Make a fist and place it thumb-side just above the navel, well below the breastbone.
Grasp your fist with the other hand and give quick, firm upward thrusts into the abdomen.
Repeat until the object is dislodged or the person can breathe, cough, or speak.
Call emergency services immediately if the person becomes unconscious, and begin CPR if you are trained.

items.heading: CPR for an adult (cardiopulmonary resuscitation)
details: Check that the scene is safe, then check for responsiveness by tapping the shoulders and shouting.
Call emergency services immediately, or have someone else call, while you start CPR.
Lay the person flat on their back on a firm surface.
Place the heel of one hand on the center of the chest, the other hand on top, fingers interlaced.
Push hard and fast, straight down about 5-6 cm, at a rate of 100-120 compressions per minute, letting the chest fully recoil between compressions.
If trained in rescue breaths, give 2 breaths after every 30 compressions; if untrained, continue hands-only compressions.
Continue until emergency help arrives or the person shows signs of life.
This is an awareness guide only - hands-on CPR training and certification is strongly recommended.

items.heading: Mild allergic reaction (skin rash, itching)
details: Wash the affected area with mild soap and cool water.
Apply a cold compress to reduce itching and swelling.
Avoid scratching, and keep the area clean and dry.
Seek emergency help immediately for facial swelling, difficulty breathing, or dizziness - these indicate a severe reaction.

items.heading: Eye irritation or a foreign particle in the eye
details: Do not rub the eye.
Rinse gently with clean water or saline solution - blinking underwater in a bowl of clean water can help.
Blink repeatedly to encourage natural tearing, which helps flush the particle out.
See a doctor immediately if the particle does not flush out, vision is affected, or there has been chemical exposure.

items.heading: Splinter removal
details: Clean the area, and a pair of tweezers, with soap and water or rubbing alcohol.
Pull the splinter out at the same angle it entered, using the sterilized tweezers.
Wash the area again after removal and apply a dab of turmeric or antiseptic.
See a doctor if the splinter is deep, breaks apart, or the area becomes infected.

items.heading: Minor electric shock
details: Do not touch the person until the power source is switched off or they are clear of it.
Switch off the mains, or unplug the appliance using a dry wooden stick or other non-conductive object if you cannot reach the switch safely.
Check if the person is breathing and responsive once they are safely separated from the source.
Call emergency services immediately for any loss of consciousness, burns, or irregular heartbeat.
For minor shocks with no serious symptoms, still consult a doctor, as internal effects are not always visible immediately.
